_note: Fresh Pavement field guide content. Source of truth for tooltips, popovers and the Field Guide page. Rider takes are our best read and should be validated by rider ratings. Photos: Wikimedia Commons, license noted per item; download into the site with attribution before shipping.

terms.one_liner: Grind off the worn top layer, lay down fresh asphalt.
steps: A milling machine grinds off the top 1.5–3 in of old asphalt.
The surface is swept and sprayed with a sticky tack coat.
A paver lays new hot-mix asphalt; rollers compact it smooth.
terms.rider_take: The good stuff. Fresh overlay is dark, tight-textured and glassy for small wheels. Best in its first few seasons.
terms.how_to_spot: Deep black, uniform surface; crisp new lane paint; often a slight lip at driveways and gutters for the first weeks.

photo_alt.caption: Milling machine grinding off old asphalt

terms.one_liner: Heat the top inch of the old road, remix it, and lay it back down.
steps: A train of heaters softens the top ~1 in of existing asphalt.
It's scraped up and mixed with a rejuvenating oil and a little new asphalt.
The mix is re-laid and rolled in one pass. Most of the road is reused on site.
terms.rider_take: Usually smooth, but the texture can be a touch coarser and greyer than a full overlay, and it won't fix deep problems underneath. Franklin St (Colfax–26th, 2026) is our test case.
terms.how_to_spot: Looks freshly paved but slightly less jet-black than new overlay; edges and gutter lines unchanged.
terms.photo_note: No good open photo found. Best source: our own photo of Franklin St.

terms.one_liner: Spray hot asphalt glue, then cover it with small stones.
steps: A truck sprays a thin layer of liquid asphalt.
A spreader drops small stone chips on top.
Rollers press the chips in; loose chips are swept up over the following days.
terms.rider_take: Rough for small wheels: buzzy, grabby and loud, with loose gravel for the first weeks. Cheap for cities, bad for skating. We cap it at Poor.
terms.how_to_spot: Every stone visible, like coarse sandpaper; grey-brown color; loose chips at the curb.

terms.one_liner: A chip seal with a slurry coat on top to fill the gaps between stones.
steps: Chip seal goes down first.
Days later, a thin slurry is squeegeed over it, filling between the chips.
terms.rider_take: Noticeably smoother than plain chip seal but still gritty. Rideable, not a destination.
terms.how_to_spot: Stones visible but sitting in a flat grey matrix; less loose gravel.

terms.one_liner: A thin, soupy coat of asphalt and fine sand spread over the road.
steps: A mix of asphalt emulsion, fine aggregate and water is made in the truck.
It's spread like a squeegee coat, about ¼ in thick.
It cures in a few hours.
terms.rider_take: Fills small cracks and looks fresh, but the surface is like fine sandpaper: grippy and a little slow.
terms.how_to_spot: Flat dark-grey coat with a fine, even sandy texture; old cracks often still faintly visible.

terms.one_liner: Rubbery sealant poured into cracks to keep water out.
steps: Cracks are blown clean with hot air.
Hot rubberized sealant is poured in and smeared over the top.
terms.rider_take: Doesn't make a street smoother. The sealant lines ('tar snakes') are little ridges and get slick when hot. We don't let it change a street's band.
terms.how_to_spot: Shiny black squiggly lines across an otherwise older road.

terms.one_liner: A spray-on oil that keeps younger asphalt from drying out.
steps: A light oil emulsion is sprayed on fairly new pavement.
It soaks in; sand is often spread so it isn't slippery.
terms.rider_take: No change in smoothness. Slippery for a day or two, then it's just preventive care.
terms.lifespan: Extends pavement life a few years
terms.how_to_spot: Road looks darker and freshly 'wet' for a few days; sand at the edges.

terms.one_liner: Broken concrete slabs are cut out and re-poured.
steps: Damaged panels are saw-cut and removed.
New concrete is poured and finished.
Joints are cut between panels so they can expand.
terms.rider_take: New slabs can be smooth, but the joints every 10–15 ft give a steady thwack-thwack on small wheels.
terms.how_to_spot: Light grey slabs with straight joints; new panels brighter than neighbors.

terms.one_liner: Tear the road out down to the base and build it back new.
steps: All asphalt (sometimes the base) is removed.
The base is rebuilt and compacted.
New asphalt or concrete is laid in layers.
terms.rider_take: Brand-new road. As good as it gets, and it stays good longest.
terms.how_to_spot: Everything new: curbs, gutters, ramps, paint.

terms.one_liner: Cut out a damaged spot and fill it with new asphalt.
steps: The bad area is cut or milled out.
Hot asphalt is placed and compacted.
terms.rider_take: Fixes a hole, but every patch edge is a bump. Patchwork streets ride rough.
terms.how_to_spot: Rectangles of darker asphalt with seams around them.

terms.one_liner: A 0–100 grade from a survey of cracks, potholes and wear.
steps: Inspectors or a camera van record every crack, patch and pothole.
Software turns that into a score: 100 = perfect, below 40 = falling apart.
terms.rider_take: Good overall signal, but it counts cracks more than bumpiness. A cracked-but-flat street can ride fine.

terms.one_liner: How much a wheel moves up and down per mile: literally, how bumpy it rides.
steps: A van with lasers drives the street and measures the surface profile.
The result is inches of up-and-down per mile. Lower = smoother.
terms.rider_take: The closest thing to ride quality we can get from city data, so we weight it more than PCI. Aurora measures it.

terms.one_liner: After paving, utilities can't dig up the street for a few years.
steps: Denver bars new cuts for 3 years after paving, except emergencies.
terms.rider_take: Good news: freshly paved streets stay patch-free for a while.

terms.one_liner: Calm enough for kids: paths, protected lanes, quiet 25-mph streets.
terms.rider_take: Relaxed riding.

terms.one_liner: Comfortable for most adults: low-speed streets or decent bike lanes.
terms.rider_take: Fine for most riders.

terms.one_liner: For confident riders: busier streets, painted lanes next to 30–35 mph traffic.
terms.rider_take: Stay alert.

terms.one_liner: High stress: fast, multi-lane traffic with little or no protection.
terms.rider_take: Avoid on a board.

terms.one_liner: A bike lane separated from cars by posts, curbs or parked cars.
terms.rider_take: Best on-street option for boards and EUCs, as long as the surface inside it is good.

terms.one_liner: A painted bike lane with an extra striped gap between you and traffic.
terms.rider_take: Better than paint alone; watch for cars crossing it.

terms.one_liner: A striped lane for bikes right next to traffic.
terms.rider_take: Often the roughest strip of the road (gutter seams, debris). Check the smoothness score.

terms.one_liner: A quiet residential street tuned for bikes with signs, speed humps and safer crossings.
terms.rider_take: Great low-stress routes; speed humps are worth knowing about on a board.

terms.one_liner: Painted bike-and-arrows symbol: you share the lane with cars.
terms.rider_take: Paint only, no space of your own.

terms.one_liner: Off-street paved path for bikes, boards and walkers, like the Cherry Creek Trail.
terms.rider_take: Often the best skating in town. Concrete trails have joints; asphalt ones are smoother.

bands.label: Fresh
bands.one_liner: Brand-new mill & overlay or rebuild, ≤2 seasons old.

bands.label: Fair
bands.one_liner: Rideable; some cracks, patches or texture.
